passage:
At nineteen, Shreya sat in her first lecture at the institute and thought, they made a mistake with my admission. She counted her classmates' answers as smarter than hers, dismissed her top marks in the first test as an easy paper, and told her roommate Yamini, 'Everyone will find out soon.' Yamini stared. 'You came third in the batch.' 'That's luck,' said Shreya.

At twenty-five, Kavitha joined a design firm and stayed until nine every night, rechecking every slide four times. When her manager praised the deck, she said, 'It only worked because I put in so many hours.' The relief lasted a night, and next morning she began over-preparing again. A senior said, 'I did the same in my first year. The hours weren't why the client liked it. Your idea was.' Kavitha half believed it and left at seven the next day.

qa.q: What did Yamini say about Shreya's rank?
qa.a: That she came third in the batch.

qa.q: How is the belief of being a fraud kept alive in both scenes?
qa.a: Shreya dismissed her top marks as an easy paper and called her third place luck, while comparing herself with her classmates. Kavitha stayed late and rechecked every slide, then said the deck worked only because of so many hours, so the cycle of relief and over-preparing began again

qa.q: What was Kavitha feeling when her manager praised her deck?
qa.a: Brief relief mixed with fear of being found out, so she explained the praise away as long hours.

qa.q: What could Kavitha try to test her belief?
qa.a: Leave earlier one day and see whether the work is still good, and ask for specific feedback about what the client valued.

grounding: Feeling like a fraud at nineteen in a top college and at twenty-five through overwork to avoid exposure.
